title: The stories you kept
hook: three stories that stuck, each with its source

segments.voice: Yesterday: looking back. Your line was how far. Did you stop on a stair or a slope and turn around? Today we look back at the stories. Day three hundred twenty-six.

Here's a test nobody warned you about. Without scrolling back, which stories from this year can you still tell? Not the facts. The stories. Some of them are gone, and that's fine; memory is a sieve. But a few have stuck. Maybe you told one at dinner. Maybe one surfaced out of nowhere on a bad day, and it helped. That's how stories have always worked. Long before anyone wrote them down, people kept the ones that were useful, and told them to their children. The ones that survive aren't random. They're the ones that stayed. Today: the stories you kept.
screen: `WHICH CAN YOU STILL TELL?` → `MEMORY IS A SIEVE.` → `THE ONES THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Let's walk through three that many people keep, and say where each came from, because each belongs to the people who kept it. First, the shipwreck. A merchant named Zeno, carrying a cargo of purple dye, loses everything in a wreck off Athens. He wanders into a bookshop, hears someone reading about Socrates, and asks where men like that can be found. The bookseller points at a passing philosopher: follow that man. Zeno went on to found the Stoic school, named for the painted porch where he taught. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, book seven. It stays because almost everyone has a wreck that turned out to be a door. Second, the carob tree. In the Talmud, an old man named Honi sees someone planting a carob tree and asks how long until it bears fruit. Seventy years, the man says. Will you live to eat it? I found carob trees in the world, the man answers; my ancestors planted them for me, and I plant for my children. Source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a. It stays because it's the best answer to why bother. Third, the mustard seed. Kisa Gotami, mad with grief, carries her dead child to the Buddha and begs for medicine. He asks her for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died. She goes door to door. Every house has lost someone. She returns with no seed, and with her grief shared. Source: the commentary on the Therigatha, verses of the early Buddhist nuns. It stays because it doesn't fix grief. It keeps it company. Three traditions, three houses. Each story is still theirs. You were a guest who got to listen.
screen: `ZENO'S WRECK BECOMES A DOOR.` · `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.` · `KISA GOTAMI'S MUSTARD SEED.` · `SAY WHERE IT CAME FROM.` · then, large: `THESE STAYED.`

segments.voice: Choose one story from this year that stayed with you. One of these three, or any other. Now tell it to yourself, silently, in three sentences: what happened, what turned, and where it comes from. Say the source too, the way we always have. Then picture who you'd tell it to today: a child, a friend, a coworker who's having a hard week. The bell holds the time.
The stories you kept. The few that stuck, each still belonging to the tradition that kept it for centuries. Today's word.
Your line: these stayed. Tell your story to one person today, in three sentences, and end with where it came from. Day three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Traditions pass on their teaching stories by retelling them, at meals, in classes, in sermons and at bedtime; people on their own path often keep a few favorites and tell them with their source.

every house had lost someone; she came back with no seed and her grief shared.

fork.setup: you're Kisa Gotami, going door to door for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died. what do you find?
options: the Buddha gives you the seed himself.
fork.reveal: no such house exists. she returns with no seed, but knowing grief is shared by everyone.

trapdoor: what you thought: stories are for children.
what it means: the ones that stay are the ones that help, kept by the people who told them.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laertius 7.2–3, Taanit 23a, and Dhammapala's commentary on the Therigatha, three different houses, each with its own telling.

notes: Zeno: Diogenes Laertius 7.2–3 (shipwreck near Piraeus with purple dye, bookshop, Xenophon's Memorabilia being read, Crates passing). Script says 'hears someone reading about Socrates'. Confirm.
Taanit 23a: Honi sees a man planting a carob tree; seventy years; 'I found carobs in the world; as my fathers planted for me, so I plant for my children.' Paraphrased; Jewish reviewer to confirm.
Kisa Gotami: Therigatha commentary (Dhammapala) and Dhammapada commentary; paraphrased. Buddhist reviewer to confirm.
These three stories were told on days 25–26, 58 and 75; 'say where it came from' echoes day 95.
